name: Sydney Opera House
label: Sydney Opera House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mrs Macquarie's Chair' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mrs Macquarie's Chair' (node/13887214): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9596872: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sydney Opera House' (226 m across).
notes: The famous sail-roofed performing arts centre on Bennelong Point.

text.description:
The Sydney Opera House fills the whole of Bennelong Point, a finger of land between Sydney Cove and Farm Cove, right beside the Royal Botanic Garden. Its roofs are a cluster of white sails set on a wide stone podium. Danish architect Jørn Utzon won the international design competition in 1957, and Queen Elizabeth II opened the building on 20 October 1973. Up close, the sails are not plain white. They are covered in more than a million tiles in two finishes, glossy white and matte cream, which gives them a faint chevron pattern that can catch the light.

This spot works best from the tip of the sandstone peninsula at Mrs Macquarie's Chair, on the Farm Cove side of the garden. From there the Opera House and the Harbour Bridge sit together in one frame across the water, with ferries passing and the city skyline behind. Guides often call it the classic postcard view, and it is free to visit. Stand a little back from the chair itself so both landmarks fit comfortably. If you want a closer, front-on view of the sails, Hickson Road Reserve and Mary Booth Lookout Reserve are two other places to try. Mrs Macquarie's Chair is in the Royal Botanic Garden, and the garden gates close around sunset, so plan your exit before you settle in for the evening.
text.geographic_location: The Opera House stands on Bennelong Point on the Sydney Harbour foreshore, next to the Royal Botanic Garden and the edge of the Sydney CBD. The Harbour Bridge is close by.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for the Royal Botanic Garden on the edge of the Sydney CBD. Mrs Macquarie's Chair is at the tip of the peninsula on the Farm Cove side. From there, the Opera House is about 742 m to the north-west in a straight line, and the walk around the cove is longer than that. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which fits the Opera House and the Harbour Bridge into one frame from here. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the sails with ferries passing in front. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for when you step back and want more of the foreground and sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Mrs Macquarie's Chair (tip of the sandstone peninsula in the Royal Botanic Garden, Farm Cove side). The Opera House and Harbour Bridge framed together across the harbour, with ferries and the city skyline behind. The Opera House is to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the horizon on a lower line so the sky and the sails get plenty of room. Put the Opera House on one side and the bridge on the other, and let the water and any passing ferry fill the gap. If you want a closer, front-on view, Hickson Road Reserve or Mary Booth Lookout Reserve are alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sails to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash them out. In dim light before sunrise, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a solid surface to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About twenty minutes before sunrise, when the sails catch the first light. Check the garden's current opening hours before you go, because the gates close around sunset.

text.access_note: The viewpoint at Mrs Macquarie's Chair is free and open to the public, but it lies inside the Royal Botanic Garden, which closes around sunset, and any Opera House tours or performances are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The walk from Mrs Macquarie's Chair to the Opera House around Farm Cove is longer than the 742 m straight-line distance given; the real route and walking time are not in the sources.
The Royal Botanic Garden is on the edge of the Sydney CBD.
Tapping to focus and lowering the exposure helps keep a bright sky from washing out the white sails.

name: Sydney Harbour Bridge
label: Sydney Harbour Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mrs Macquarie's Chair' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mrs Macquarie's Chair' (node/13887214): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3178788: large area 'Sydney Harbour Bridge' (1525 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The iconic steel arch bridge, nicknamed the Coathanger.

text.description:
The Sydney Harbour Bridge is a steel arch bridge linking the city centre with the North Shore. It opened in 1932 and is nicknamed "the Coathanger". The arch spans 504 metres and rises 134 metres above the water. It is held together by around six million hand-driven rivets and is framed at each end by granite-faced pylons. It photographs well because the arch is such a clear, strong shape, and because from the right place you can fit it into the same frame as the Opera House and the harbour.

The best view for that is Mrs Macquarie's Chair, at the tip of the peninsula inside the Royal Botanic Garden. Several guides call it the single best place to get the bridge and the Opera House together. From there the bridge sits across the water to the north-west, with the city rising behind. Because you are a good way back, the bridge will look fairly small at first. Take a test shot, then zoom in a little and decide what matters most to you: the whole arch, or the arch and the Opera House as a pair.

If you have time for a second angle, Milsons Point Ferry Wharf shows the bridge filling the frame from the north side. Observatory Hill Park gives you the bridge with the old sandstone buildings of The Rocks in the foreground.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses Sydney Harbour between Dawes Point in The Rocks, next to the city centre, and Milsons Point on the lower North Shore.
text.directions_text: Start from the Sydney city centre and make your way to the Royal Botanic Garden by whatever local means suit you. Walk out along the shore from Farm Cove to the tip of the peninsula, where Mrs Macquarie's Chair is. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the bridge, the Opera House and the harbour in one frame. Try 2x or the telephoto if you want the arch larger. The ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the bridge look small and far away from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Mrs Macquarie's Chair (tip of the peninsula inside the Royal Botanic Garden, reached via Farm Cove). The bridge arch and the Opera House together in one frame, with the harbour and city behind. The bridge itself lies to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the arch along one of the horizontal lines. Keep the Opera House to one side so the two do not compete, and leave some water in the foreground. For a different view, try Milsons Point Ferry Wharf, where the bridge fills the frame from the north side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. At dusk, night mode can help, but rest your phone on a wall or railing to keep it steady. Live Photos can catch ferries crossing the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset and late afternoon, especially under dramatic skies. Sunrise also works.

text.access_note: The bridge is a working road, rail and pedestrian crossing, and Mrs Macquarie's Chair is inside the Royal Botanic Garden, so check the official site for opening times, and for any bridge walkway or pylon lookout, before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From Mrs Macquarie's Chair the bridge looks fairly small at 1x, so a gentle zoom (about 2x) can help.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) makes distant subjects look smaller and further away.
Resting a phone on a wall or railing helps keep night shots steady.

name: The Rocks
label: The Rocks
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Observatory Hill' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Observatory Hill Park' (way/55218510): middle (280 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5729505: large area 'The Rocks' (1118 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic harbourside quarter with sandstone lanes and old pubs.

text.description:
The Rocks is a historic area of Sydney's city centre, on the southern shore of the harbour just beside the Harbour Bridge. The area was settled shortly after the colony's formation in 1788, first with simple wattle-and-daub houses and later with local sandstone, which gives the area its name. Many of those sandstone buildings survive. In the 1970s residents and unions fought off plans to demolish most of the district, which is why the old streets are still here today.

The best way to photograph it on a phone is to step back and look down over it. From Observatory Hill, the sandstone rooftops and streets fill the foreground and the Harbour Bridge arches across the background. That gives you the old and the new in one frame, which is hard to get at street level. Guides describe the hill as a quieter spot, because the short climb deters some visitors.

The west-facing lawn near the rotunda and the fig trees is the place to aim for. The figs make a natural frame at the edge of the picture. The hill can be busy with wedding parties at weekends, so check the foreground before you shoot and move a few steps if someone wanders in. If you have time afterwards, walk down into the streets for close-ups of the terraces. Gloucester Street has a row of sandstone houses with arched windows, and Hickson Road Reserve shows the waterfront with the bridge overhead. Conditions change, so take a quick look on the day.
text.geographic_location: The Rocks is on the southern shore of Sydney Harbour, immediately north-west of the Sydney CBD. It sits beside Circular Quay and at the southern foot of the Harbour Bridge.
text.directions_text: Circular Quay station is within walking distance of The Rocks, so start there and head west into the old streets. Allow a little extra for the short climb up Observatory Hill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the rooftops and the bridge together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the foreground lawn and trees as a frame. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the bridge or a cluster of sandstone roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Observatory Hill (west-facing lawn near the rotunda and fig trees). The Rocks' sandstone rooftops and streets in the foreground, with the Harbour Bridge arching behind them. The centre of The Rocks lies to the east of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the bridge on an upper line, with the rooftops filling the lower third. Use the fig trees or the edge of the lawn as a frame at the side. If the lawn is crowded, shoot from a slightly different angle rather than waiting. For a different view, Hickson Road Reserve shows the waterfront with ferries passing under the bridge's southern approach.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge or the brightest part of the sky to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the sandstone does not wash out. Try a Live Photo if people or birds are moving through the scene, and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, around golden hour (4-6pm), when the western light falls on the rooftops.

text.access_note: Observatory Hill is an open public park; it is worth checking the official site before you go in case of events or closures.
claims_not_in_sources: Fig trees on Observatory Hill can act as a natural frame at the edge of a phone photo.
Observatory Hill is reached by a short uphill walk from the streets of The Rocks.
Setting exposure on the bright sky helps keep sky colour and avoids washed-out sandstone.
Weekend wedding parties on Observatory Hill may appear in the foreground.

name: Circular Quay
label: Circular Quay
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cahill Expressway' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Cahill Expressway nearest the subject (our map tiles); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1092910: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Ferry harbour with views of the Opera House and the bridge.

text.description: Circular Quay is Sydney's main harbour front: a former shipping port that is now a ferry hub, public piazza and busy tourist precinct on the northern edge of the city centre. It photographs well because the ferry wharves, the water, the Sydney Harbour Bridge and the Sydney Opera House all sit close together. For the best view, go up to the Cahill Expressway, the elevated walkway above the Quay, which is the recommended viewpoint. From up there you look down over the wharves and across the Quay with the bridge and the Opera House in the background, all in one frame. The Quay was built in 1837–1844 by reconstructing the southern end of Sydney Cove with an artificial shoreline. The first ferry wharf followed in 1879, and ferries have dominated the harbour since the 1890s. The Cahill Expressway itself opened on 24 March 1958, so the viewpoint is part of the Quay's later story too. From the walkway, keep the ferries in the lower part of the picture and let the two landmarks sit higher up. Wait for a ferry to move into a gap for a livelier shot. At street level, cruise ships moored in the harbour can block the Opera House view, so the walkway is the more reliable choice. If it is closed or too crowded, Circular Quay Wharf 3 gives a street-level view of the ferries with the bridge behind them. Campbell's Cove is another option, but it is always busy.
text.geographic_location: Circular Quay sits on the northern shoreline of Sydney's central business district, in Sydney Cove between Bennelong Point (the Opera House) and The Rocks. The Cahill Expressway runs along its southern side, above the railway station.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Circular Quay railway station. The lifts up to the Cahill Expressway walkway are near the station. Once up, stop near the George Street end toward The Rocks. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the Quay, the bridge and the Opera House together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the wharves and sky. Use the telephoto (2x–5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Opera House or the bridge on their own.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Cahill Expressway (elevated walkway above Circular Quay, reached by the lifts near the station; stop near the George Street end toward The Rocks). A high, open angle over the ferry wharves and the Quay, with the Opera House and Harbour Bridge both in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper line, so the ferries and water fill the lower part of the picture. Put the bridge on one side and the Opera House on the other. Wait for a ferry to cross the frame. If the walkway is not available, Circular Quay Wharf 3 gives a street-level shot of the ferry terminals with the bridge arching behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge or the Opera House to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the buildings keep their detail. Try a Live Photo to catch a ferry pulling away. Use panorama only if the walkway is quiet, because people walking past can spoil the join.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually kinder than midday. Looking north, you are often shooting towards the sun, so check the sky and adjust the exposure slider.

text.access_note: The walkway is reached by lifts near the station and is understood to be free to use, but check the official site before you go for opening hours and any closures.
claims_not_in_sources: In Sydney the sun is mostly in the northern sky, so a view looking north is often towards the light, especially around midday.
Early morning and late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.
Ferries come and go regularly, so the foreground changes from minute to minute.
People walking past on a busy walkway can spoil a panorama.

name: Darling Harbour
label: Darling Harbour
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pier 7' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'The Pier Apartments' (way/52751260): middle (212 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Waterfront leisure precinct with the skyline across the water.

text.description: Darling Harbour is the busy waterfront playground adjacent to Sydney's city centre, built around Cockle Bay. It was originally called Long Cove. It took its present name in 1826 from Governor Ralph Darling, who held office from 1825 to 1831. By the mid-to-late 1980s the old rail yards and wharves had become run-down, and the area was redeveloped as a pedestrian and tourist precinct. For a phone photographer the appeal is the whole sweep of the bay: the western shore, the water in front, and the city's towers rising behind. The best-known angle is the wide panorama from Pier 7, on the north side near the Foxtel building. It looks across to the western shore of Cockle Bay with the central business district skyline above it. One guide rates it the best wide view of that side of the bay. It is free to stand there and best later in the day, around sunset and for up to an hour afterwards. The west shore is being redeveloped (the old Harbourside shopping centre was demolished in 2023), so details of the view may change from year to year. If you want a different angle, Pyrmont Bridge gives a wide view of the bay and waterfront, and Observatory Hill gives a higher, quieter look down over Darling Harbour. Event nights such as the fireworks and Vivid bring big crowds to Cockle Bay, so arrive early to get a good position.
text.geographic_location: Darling Harbour sits right beside Sydney's city centre, stretching north from Chinatown along both sides of Cockle Bay, with Pyrmont on its western side. The Pier 7 viewpoint is on the northern side of the bay, near the Foxtel building.
text.directions_text: Darling Harbour is served by the Inner West Light Rail, with stops at Paddy's Markets, Convention, Exhibition and Pyrmont Bay, and Town Hall is the nearest train station. Confirm the exact spot on the ground, using the Foxtel building as your landmark. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole western shore of Cockle Bay, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural skyline view. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), use it to pick out a single group of towers or the lights on the far shore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Pier 7 (North spot, near the Foxtel building). A wide panorama of the western shore of Cockle Bay and the central business district skyline. From there the main subject, Darling Harbour and Cockle Bay, lies to the south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the waterline on the lower third, so the shore and skyline fill the rest of the frame with the sky on top. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean. If you want a different angle, Pyrmont Bridge gives a wide view of the bay with the bridge in the frame, and Observatory Hill gives a higher, quieter view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the skyline to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Once the light fades, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone still. Panorama mode also works for a very wide sweep, as long as you pan slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The second half of the day is best, around sunset and for up to an hour afterwards. On fireworks or Vivid nights, arrive early to get a good position.

text.access_note: Pier 7 is a public place with no charge to stand there, but check the official site before you go in case of event closures or restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: Night mode helps once the light fades after sunset, when the city's lights come on.
Walking from the stand-here point at Pier 7 to the Darling Harbour waterfront takes about 31 minutes (calculated from the distance).
The Foxtel building is a useful landmark for finding the viewpoint on the ground.

name: Luna Park Sydney
label: Luna Park Sydney
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hickson Road Reserve' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hickson Road Reserve' (way/193989909): middle (92 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2916623: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Luna Park' (424 m across).
notes: Amusement park with its giant smiling face entrance at Milsons Point.

text.description:
Luna Park Sydney is a heritage-listed amusement park at Milsons Point, on the northern shore of Sydney Harbour. It opened on 4 October 1935 on a site that had been used to build steelwork for the Harbour Bridge. Its best-known feature is the big smiling entrance face, set between two Art Deco towers, which has been rebuilt and reworked over the decades. The park closed and reopened several times before settling into its current run in 2004.

It photographs well because the colourful rides and signage sit close to the Harbour Bridge, with water in front. The map's stand-here point is Hickson Road Reserve, on the opposite side of the harbour. From there you see the park and the bridge together in one frame. A photographer's guide rates this the spot most likely to give the best bridge-and-Luna-Park shots, and it is an easy walk from Circular Quay. Luna Park looks small at that distance, so zoom in a little and let the bridge and water fill the rest of the frame.

If you want the face entrance itself, with the park's signage around it, go over to the Luna Park side. You can also shoot from the waterfront edge at Luna Park Wharf, with the bridge rising behind the park. Photography on the rides is generally not allowed.
text.geographic_location: Luna Park is at Milsons Point on the northern shore of Sydney Harbour, close to the northern end of the Harbour Bridge and next to North Sydney Olympic Pool.
text.directions_text: Hickson Road Reserve is an easy walk from Circular Quay. Once you are at the reserve, Luna Park is straight across the water to the north. To photograph the park from its own side, travel across the harbour to Milsons Point and check the route before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start on the default lens (1x) to take in the bridge, the water and the park together. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Luna Park closer. Avoid ultra-wide (0.5x) here, because it makes the park even smaller in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hickson Road Reserve. The park from across the harbour, with the Harbour Bridge and Luna Park together in the background; a long exposure can smooth the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on a lower line so the bridge and the colourful park sit together above the water. Keep some foreground water in the frame. For an alternative, Luna Park Wharf, at the waterfront edge, gives a view of the park with the bridge rising behind it. The famous face entrance is better shot from the park side, framed against the signage.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the park to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright lights and sky are not washed out. At dusk, try night mode and brace your phone on a railing or wall to keep it steady. A long exposure can smooth the water. Take a few shots, as boat wakes change the surface.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The best time of day varies, so check sunset timing for your visit. Dusk is worth trying if you want the water to look smooth and the park lit up.

text.access_note: Hickson Road Reserve is a public park, and visiting Luna Park's grounds is free, with payment only for rides; photography on rides is generally not allowed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Night mode on a phone uses a longer exposure and can smooth moving water.
Bracing a phone on a railing or wall helps keep it steady in low light.
Luna Park's lights are on after dark, so dusk can show it lit up.
Boat wakes change the look of the water between shots.

name: Martin Place
label: Martin Place
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'General Post Office' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Sydney General Post Office' (way/282238525): middle (107 m across); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q761633 (coordinate location).
notes: Pedestrian plaza lined with historic buildings in the CBD.

text.description: Martin Place is a pedestrian mall in the heart of Sydney's business district, often called the city's civic heart. It runs between George Street and Macquarie Street and is lined with heritage buildings, banks and towers. The easiest first photo is at the General Post Office on the south side, where a long line of sandstone arches gives the picture depth and a sense of history. The building was started in 1863 and finished in 1891, in a Venetian-Italianate style. The mall took its name a year later, in 1892, after Sir James Martin, a former Premier of New South Wales. Further along, between the Post Office and Challis House, stands the Sydney Cenotaph. It was dedicated on 8 August 1927 and is made of Moruya granite, with bronze figures of a soldier and a sailor. It makes a strong second subject, with the sandstone building behind it. The mall has been closed to traffic in stages since 1971, so you can stand and frame a shot without worrying about cars. In the run-up to Christmas, the tree and Santa displays bring crowds and structures that can block the Cenotaph and Post Office views. Guides suggest going after about 9 PM, when it thins out. Ceremonies such as ANZAC Day dawn services can also limit access around the Cenotaph. If you want a wide view of the whole mall with the towers around it, walk a little east and shoot along the plaza at dusk.
text.geographic_location: Martin Place is in the Sydney central business district, running between George Street and Macquarie Street. The General Post Office fills the southern side of the western end.
text.directions_text: Head for the Sydney central business district and the General Post Office on Martin Place. The mall also has entrances to the Martin Place railway station below street level. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the row of arches and the wide street scene. Switch to 2x or the telephoto lens if your phone has one for the Cenotaph's statues. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only when the square is crowded and you need to fit everything in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at General Post Office. The long line of sandstone arches of the GPO, which gives the square depth and a sense of its historic character. Turn east and the main stretch of the mall lies ahead of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Stand at one end of the arcade and let the arches recede into the distance, so the repeating shapes lead the eye. Switch on gridlines to keep the columns upright. For a second picture, move to the Sydney Cenotaph and frame the granite tomb and bronze figures with the sandstone building behind them. For a wide view of the whole mall with the towers and facades, walk along the plaza and shoot from there at dusk or night.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines. Tap the arches to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sandstone keeps its colour in bright sky. At dusk or night, use night mode and rest your elbows against a wall or your body to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Outside the Christmas period, any time you can get a clear view works. In late November to Christmas Eve, guides suggest going after about 9 PM, when the crowds thin out. Avoid ANZAC Day mornings if you want to photograph the Cenotaph.

text.access_note: Martin Place is a pedestrian mall, but events and ceremonies can restrict access near the Cenotaph, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The mall can be walked into at any time, with no entry charge for the open street.
A phone held against a wall or your body is steadier for night-mode shots.
Ultra-wide lenses can stretch or tilt vertical lines near the edges of the frame.

name: Sydney Tower
label: Sydney Tower
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/197801072: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sydney Tower' (41 m across).
notes: The tallest structure in the city, with a viewing deck.

text.description: Sydney Tower is the tallest structure in Sydney, rising 309 m above the central business district. It stands on Market Street between Pitt and Castlereagh Streets and sits on top of the Westfield Sydney shopping centre. You may also hear it called Centrepoint Tower or the Sydney Tower Eye. Architect Donald Crone designed it, and the public were first let in on 25 September 1981. Before it was built, the city's height limit was set lower to leave room for the harbour's flying boats. The golden turret near the top is the part that catches the eye, and the observation deck sits about 250 m above the ground. It photographs well because it is a single tall shape that shows up above the surrounding streets. From the base you get a strong upward view, with the shaft narrowing towards the turret and spire. Standing right at its foot, you will not fit the whole tower in unless you use the widest lens on your phone and tilt the phone up. For a full-length shot, walk back along the nearby streets until the spire fits in the frame. Then try the zoom to pick out the golden turret on its own. Expect busy pavements around the entrances, so take your time and keep clear of the doors.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of Sydney's central business district, on Market Street between Pitt and Castlereagh Streets, above the Westfield Sydney shopping centre and close to Pitt Street Mall.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Pitt Street Mall in the centre of Sydney's central business district. The tower is on Market Street between Pitt and Castlereagh Streets, and can be reached from Pitt Street Mall, Market Street or Castlereagh Street. The phone icon on the map is at the tower itself, so once you are at its base there is no further walk (about 0 minutes on foot). The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the tower's height from close up. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view from further back. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to isolate the golden turret and spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo is a steep look up the shaft, so keep your phone close to upright and tilt it back gently. For a fuller view of the whole tower, walk a short way back along the surrounding streets.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the shaft up with a vertical line so it does not lean too much. Let the tower run diagonally or up the centre of the frame, with the spire near the top edge. Leave a little sky above the tip. If you walk back, use the default lens (1x) or zoom to include the golden turret.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. Use night mode after dark and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing, or brace your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually works well, when the sky has colour and the tower is easier to separate from it. Early morning tends to have fewer people at the base.

text.access_note: The tower is open to the public, but the observation deck needs a pass and the SKYWALK is only available on booked tours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Royal Botanic Garden Sydney
label: Royal Botanic Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mrs Macquarie's Chair' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mrs Macquarie's Chair' (node/13887214): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3744999: large area 'Royal Botanic Garden' (1237 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Waterfront gardens beside the Opera House.

text.description: The Royal Botanic Garden covers about 30 hectares on the shore of Farm Cove, on the eastern edge of the city centre. It opened in 1816 and is the oldest scientific institution in Australia. Even before that, in 1788, the first European farm on the continent was started on this ground. For photographs, the best-known spot is Mrs Macquarie's Chair, a sandstone seat at the tip of the peninsula at the east end of the garden. From there the Opera House and the Sydney Harbour Bridge sit together across the water, usually with ferries passing, so one frame holds both landmarks. Guides often call it the classic postcard view. Behind you the garden's lawns, palms and old trees give good material for softer, greener pictures if the crowds are thick at the water's edge. The garden and the neighbouring Domain are open every day of the year and entry is free, so you can wander at your own pace. Mrs Macquarie's Point, on the same headland, gives a wide harbour view with the sandstone edge in the foreground, and is a good alternative if the chair is busy. Early morning and sunset are the best times to come, and tour groups are fewer then. Check the current closing time on the day before planning a sunset visit.
text.geographic_location: In the Royal Botanic Garden at Farm Cove, on the eastern edge of Sydney's central business district, beside Sydney Harbour. Mrs Macquarie's Chair is at the tip of the peninsula at the garden's eastern end.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is given for this spot, so head east from the Sydney city centre towards the harbour edge. The middle of the garden lies about 700 m to the south-west of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the Opera House and the Harbour Bridge both fit in the frame. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the sandstone seat and a big sky as well. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to bring the two landmarks closer together.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (sandstone seat at the tip of the peninsula at the east end of the garden). The Opera House and Sydney Harbour Bridge framed together across the water, with ferries on the harbour. The garden itself lies to the south-west of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on a lower line, with the two landmarks along the upper third. Keep the horizon level. For a different picture, include the curved sandstone seat in the foreground with the 0.5x lens. Mrs Macquarie's Point, on the same headland, is an alternative with a wide harbour view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the landmarks to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour. Take a few shots as a ferry passes. Live Photos can help you pick the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or sunset, when tour groups are fewer. Check the garden's current closing time before going for sunset.

text.access_note: The garden and the Domain are open every day and access is free, but check the official site for current closing times before you go.

name: Queen Victoria Building
label: Queen Victoria Buildin
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'George Street and Park Street corner' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of George Street and Park Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/40717424: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Queen Victoria Building' (192 m across).
notes: Romanesque Revival shopping arcade with a grand domed roof.

text.description:
The Queen Victoria Building, often called the QVB, fills a whole city block in the middle of Sydney. It was designed by the Scottish-born architect George McRae in a Romanesque Revival style and built between 1893 and 1898. It measures about 30 metres wide by 190 metres long, so it is a very long frontage to fit into a phone frame. It was built as a marketplace, and it was restored and returned to its original use in the late twentieth century. It is now heritage-listed.

It photographs well because of the detail. There are columns, arches and balustrades, and a copper-sheathed central dome with smaller domes and cupolas along the roofline. Inside, stained-glass windows and arched skylights let light into the central area.

The standard outside shot is taken from the George Street and Park Street corner, looking along the George Street frontage. The building sits in the frame with the street leading the eye towards it. It is a free public footpath spot. If you have time, Bicentennial Plaza at the southern end gives you the statue of Queen Victoria in the foreground. Inside, the central atrium is worth a look upwards, though it is a working shopping centre, so keep your photography discreet. Check for roadworks on George Street before you go, as the street has been affected by building work in the past.
text.geographic_location: The building is on George Street in the Sydney central business district. It fills the block bounded by George, Market, York and Druitt streets, next to the Town Hall.
text.directions_text: Head for the Sydney central business district and the corner of George Street and Park Street. Shoot from there, looking north. Check for roadworks or street closures before you set off. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) from the corner to fit the long George Street frontage. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the domes and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of George Street and Park Street (corner facing the building's George Street frontage). The Queen Victoria Building's exterior and Romanesque facade along George Street, framed from the corner.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them so the walls do not lean. Let the footpath and street lead the eye towards the facade. If you want a second view, Bicentennial Plaza at the southern end puts the statue of Queen Victoria in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands and take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go outside the busiest shopping hours if you can, so there are fewer people on the footpath. In the evening, try night mode on the lit facade.

text.access_note: The corner is an open public footpath. The interior is a shopping centre, so check the official site before you go for opening hours and any photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Outside the busiest shopping hours there are usually fewer people on the footpath around the building.
The facade may be lit in the evening, which suits night mode.
Gridlines on a phone help keep vertical building edges straight.

name: Barangaroo Reserve
label: Barangaroo Reserve
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Stargazer Lawn' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Stargazer Lawn' (way/487542915): middle (142 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2025307: large area 'Barangaroo' (1213 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Landscaped headland park on the harbour foreshore.

text.description: Barangaroo Reserve is the large harbourside park at the north-western edge of Sydney's central business district, close to the southern end of the Sydney Harbour Bridge. It is named after Barangaroo, a Kamaraygal woman who was the second wife of Bennelong; the wider area took her name in October 2007. Long before the docks, the shoreline here was used by the Cadigal people for fishing and hunting, and shell middens nearby point to occupation going back around 6,000 years. The park is worth a stop for photographs because the land rises to a headland. From the lawn at the top of the headland, which guides point to as Stargazer Lawn, you get a wide view with Anzac Bridge to the west and the Sydney Harbour Bridge to the north, so both bridges can sit in one frame. Lifts near Munn's Slipway and The Cutaway save the climb. Lower down, the sandstone ledges and steps make good textured foreground against open water. Sunset is reported to be busy, so arrive early if you want a clear spot at the edge of the lawn. Drone use is restricted, so check local rules before flying one. For an alternative, Wulugul Walk shows the Harbour Bridge across the water with sandstone ledges in front.
text.geographic_location: Barangaroo Reserve is on the Sydney Harbour shoreline at the north-western edge of the central business district, in the Barangaroo and Millers Point area, close to the southern end of the Sydney Harbour Bridge.
text.directions_text: Head for the north-western edge of the Sydney central business district, close to the southern end of the Sydney Harbour Bridge. Barangaroo Reserve itself is about 420 m to the south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit Anzac Bridge and the Sydney Harbour Bridge into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Harbour Bridge on its own.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Stargazer Lawn (top of the headland, reached by the lifts near Munn's Slipway or The Cutaway). A wide frame with Anzac Bridge to the west and the Sydney Harbour Bridge to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon on a gridline, with a bridge on each side of the frame and the harbour in between. Walk to the edge of the lawn to avoid heads and railings in the picture. If you have time, go down to Wulugul Walk for the Harbour Bridge across the water with sandstone ledges in the foreground, or to Marrinawi Cove for sandstone steps leading to open water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridges to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the colours do not wash out. Try panorama mode for a sweep across both bridges, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is reported to be busy here, so arrive well before it to get a good spot. After dusk, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep the phone steady.

text.access_note: Open public parkland, reported as open 24 hours and free to enter, but check the official site before you go for any closures or local rules, including those on drones.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) is the best way to fit both bridges into one frame from the lawn.
In the evening the sun sets in the west, towards Anzac Bridge, so that side of the sky is brightest around sunset.
Resting the phone on a wall or railing helps keep night shots steady.
The lawn at the top of the headland is Stargazer Lawn.

name: Mrs Macquarie's Chair
label: Mrs Macquarie's Chair
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mrs Macquarie's Point' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mrs Macquarie's Point / Yurong' (node/13816944): point; moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/13887214: the OpenStreetMap point 'Mrs Macquarie's Chair'.
notes: Sandstone bench with the classic view of the Opera House and the bridge.

text.description:
Mrs Macquarie's Chair is a sandstone rock cut into the shape of a bench, on the peninsula known as Mrs Macquarie's Point, beside the Royal Botanic Garden. Convicts carved it by hand in 1810 for Elizabeth Macquarie, wife of Governor Lachlan Macquarie. Folklore says she liked to sit here and watch for ships arriving from Britain. Above the seat is a stone inscription about Mrs Macquarie's Road, which was completed on 13 June 1816 and measured 3 miles and 377 yards.

It photographs well because the point looks across the water to the Sydney Opera House and the Harbour Bridge, with the harbour between them. The bench itself is busy at peak times, so this map suggests the lower walking path on the Farm Cove shore as a quieter option. From the path you get the same view from a lower position, close to the water. The chair is a little further up, so check which of the two you are aiming for. If you want a different angle, moving slightly left or right can give a fresh composition.

On the lower path, keep a little of the water's edge in the foreground so the picture has depth. Wait for a gap in the crowd if you shoot from the bench. Sun direction depends on the time of day and the season, so check the sun position for your visit before you plan a sunrise or sunset shot.
text.geographic_location: On Mrs Macquarie's Point, a peninsula in Sydney Harbour on the edge of The Domain, next to the Royal Botanic Garden. It sits between Farm Cove and the water towards Garden Island, east of the Opera House.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head for the Royal Botanic Garden and The Domain and walk to Mrs Macquarie's Point. Once you are on the lower path, the chair is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the Opera House and Harbour Bridge together with the harbour between them. Try 2x or more on the telephoto to pick out the Opera House roof shells on their own. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, because the landmarks will look smaller.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Mrs Macquarie's Point (lower walking path on the Farm Cove shore, below the chair). The same Opera House and Harbour Bridge view as from the chair, but from a lower position along the water. The chair is to the south-east and a little higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the horizon on a line, with the Opera House and Bridge on the left or right thirds. Keep a strip of water or the shoreline in the foreground. If the bench is too crowded, this lower path is the quieter choice. The chair is a good alternative for a frame from the sandstone bench itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the Opera House to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the white shells keep their detail. A short panorama along the shore can also work, if you hold the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the sun position on the day of your visit. Early or late in the day is usually nicer for colour and softer light, but it is also busier. Check the opening times and access rules before you plan a sunset visit.

text.access_note: The point is part of The Domain, near the Royal Botanic Garden. Access can be tricky after dark or during events, so check the official site before you go.

name: Art Gallery of New South Wales
label: Art Gallery of NSW
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Art Gallery Road' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Art Gallery Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1265404795: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Art Gallery of New South Wales' (459 m across).
notes: Major art museum on the edge of the Domain.

text.description: The Art Gallery of New South Wales sits in The Domain, the parkland area of Sydney, and it is one of the largest public galleries in Australia. For a phone photo, the best-looking side is the front. Here the columned sandstone portico of the 1909 building, Naala Nura, stands beside the low glass pavilions of Naala Badu. The old stone and the modern glass together make a simple, balanced picture. The gallery began life as the New South Wales Academy of Art in 1872, and the permanent building was designed by the government architect Walter Liberty Vernon, with the first galleries opening in 1897. Two equestrian statues by Gilbert Bayes were placed in front of the main facade in 1926, and they are worth looking out for when you frame the entrance. The best place to take the shot is Art Gallery Road, at the pedestrian crossing in front of the gallery. From the far side of the road you can stand back far enough to fit the whole portico in, and the crossing gives you a clear, safe spot to do it. If you have time, the gallery's front also looks good from across the parkland of The Domain, and the outdoor sculpture plaza, Pearl and Ming Tee Lee Plaza, gives you sculpture in the foreground with the building behind. Keep the phone level, use the gridlines to keep the columns upright, and take a few frames in case people walk through.
text.geographic_location: The gallery is in The Domain, the parkland area of Sydney, and its sandstone front faces Art Gallery Road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is close to this spot, so head for The Domain in Sydney and make your way to Art Gallery Road. From there the gallery is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the crossing, which should fit the portico and the glass pavilions together. If you have to stand close to the kerb, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit it all in. Use telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter picture of the columns or the statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Art Gallery Road (across the road from the sandstone front, at the pedestrian crossing in front of the gallery). The columned sandstone portico of Naala Nura, the 1909 building, with the low glass pavilions of Naala Badu visible alongside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the portico in the centre and let the glass pavilions fill one side, so the old and new buildings sit together in one frame. Turn on gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines. For a different view, try The Domain, across the parkland, or the sculpture plaza, with its sculptures in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sandstone, then pull the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright and the stone looks washed out. Avoid flash, and stay on the pavement rather than the road when you step back for the wide shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day usually suits pale sandstone best, and a quieter moment makes it easier to get a clean frame without people on the crossing.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be photographed from the public street, and general entry to the gallery is usually free, but check the official site before you go, as some temporary exhibitions restrict photos.
