name: Sydney Town Hall
label: Sydney Town Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'George Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of George Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/104948253: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sydney Town Hall' (114 m across).
notes: Ornate Victorian civic building on George Street.

text.description:
Sydney Town Hall is a grand sandstone building on George Street, in the middle of the city centre. It was built in stages between 1869 and 1889 in the Second Empire style, which gives it its pavilions and clock tower. It is heritage-listed and part of a group of old buildings that includes the Queen Victoria Building and St Andrew's Cathedral. The Town Hall also stands on the site of Sydney's first permanent cemetery, which was in use from 1792 to 1820, and its steps are a popular meeting place.

It photographs well because the front is symmetrical, so a straight-on shot looks tidy and balanced. Modern towers rise behind the old stonework, which shows how much the city has changed. The best-known view is from the pavement directly across George Street, where the whole facade and the clock tower fit in one frame. Guides suggest a wide lens to fit it all in, and on a phone that means the ultra-wide (0.5x).

If you have time for a second shot, try the Queen Victoria Building side, which puts both landmarks together. A close, low-angle view of the front steps with the clock tower rising above also works. Keep the phone level so the tower doesn't lean, and allow for people walking through your frame, since this is a busy part of town.
text.geographic_location: In the Sydney central business district at 483 George Street, directly opposite the Queen Victoria Building and alongside St Andrew's Cathedral.
text.directions_text: Head for the Town Hall at 483 George Street, in the city centre opposite the Queen Victoria Building. Town Hall station sits directly below the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full facade and clock tower in one frame from across the street. If you are further back, the default lens (1x) gives a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the clock tower or the stonework detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on George Street (the pavement directly across from the Town Hall's full front). A straight-on, full-frontal view of the sandstone facade and the clock tower, with modern towers around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the facade up with the middle of the frame, so the symmetry shows. Hold the phone upright and level, as tilting it upwards makes the tower lean back. For a different shot, the Queen Victoria Building side shows the Town Hall and the Queen Victoria Building together, and a low, close angle at the front steps makes the clock tower rise above you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sandstone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour and detail. Wait a moment for a gap in the pedestrians before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sandstone takes on warm, directional light.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the public pavement on George Street, but opening hours and access inside vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: George Street pavements in the city centre are usually busy with pedestrians during the day.
Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean backwards, and gridlines help keep it level.
From the George Street pavement across from the Town Hall, the building lies to the south-west of the stand-here point.
Town Hall station is directly below the building (from the general description of the site; no station was listed in the spot data).

name: St Mary's Cathedral
label: St Mary's Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hyde Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hyde Park' (relation/2030042): edge nearest the subject (809 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/16749128: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Mary's Cathedral' (127 m across).
notes: Gothic Revival Catholic cathedral beside Hyde Park.

text.description:
St Mary's Cathedral is the Catholic cathedral of Sydney, a big Gothic Revival church in sandstone on College Street. William Wardell designed it, and building ran from 1866 to 1928. The two front towers stood squared-off for decades, and their spires were only added in 2000. That is why the front now looks so complete, with twin spires either side of the central tower.

The classic exterior photo is taken from Hyde Park, on the east side of the park, across College Street from the cathedral. A long reflecting pool sits there, though it is worth checking its exact position on the map. If you stand low and centred beside it, you get a symmetrical view of the western facade and towers, with the building mirrored in the water. Guides rate this as the best outside view, and it works well on a phone because everything is simple and straight-on.

The park itself has a story. Before it was parkland, the site was a barren area where bricks were made for Governor Macquarie's buildings, and the first St Mary's church looked out over it.

If the pool is rippled or crowded, two other spots work. College Street gives a straight-on view of the full front and both spires. The Domain, to the north, lets you zoom in on the towers from a distance. Photograph the outside only unless signs say otherwise inside, and never during services.
text.geographic_location: St Mary's Cathedral stands on College Street, near the eastern edge of Sydney's central business district. Hyde Park lies directly across the road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a map for the best way to reach the eastern edge of the city centre beside Hyde Park. Check the exact position of the reflecting pool in Hyde Park on the map before you set up. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the pool and want both towers and the reflection in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched look from further back. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is best for the spires and façade details, or from The Domain.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hyde Park (east side of the park, across College Street from the cathedral, at the long reflecting pool). The cathedral's western facade and towers, mirrored in the long reflecting pool in front of it. Keep yourself centred on the pool so the two sides match.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the central tower on the middle line. Crouch and hold the phone low, close to the water, so the reflection fills the lower part of the frame. For a different view, try College Street for a straight-on shot of the whole front and both spires, or The Domain to the north with the telephoto for a compressed view of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the cathedral to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and stone keep their detail. Keep the phone level so the towers stay upright. If the building is lit up for Vivid Sydney, try night mode and rest your elbows on something steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the water is calmest and the light is soft.

text.access_note: The park and the street views are open public space, but rules for photography inside the cathedral can vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Museum of Contemporary Art Australia
label: Museum of Contemporary
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cahill Walk' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Cahill Walk nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/16599528: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum of Contemporary Art' (128 m across).
notes: Art deco museum on Circular Quay.

text.description:
The Museum of Contemporary Art Australia (MCA) fills a former Maritime Services Board building on the western side of Circular Quay, in The Rocks. It is a six-storey block of light orange-brown stone in a plain, stripped-back classical style with Art Deco touches. A slightly projecting clock tower with a small cupola and three flagpoles sits at the centre. A newer wing in black, white and brown stone was added when the museum reopened in 2012, so you get old and new side by side. The museum as an institution dates from 1991. It grew out of a bequest in the 1943 will of the artist JW Power.

The building photographs well because it sits right on the waterfront, with a broad lawn, ferry slips and the water in front of it. A good, less-crowded exterior view is from Cahill Walk, the elevated walkway above Circular Quay Station. From here you look down on the museum's harbour side, with the ferry wharves and water in the foreground. It is free to reach on foot and is usually less crowded than the quayside. You stand with the museum to the north.

If you would rather be at street level, Circular Quay shows the pale Art Deco front as you arrive by ferry, with the Opera House across the cove. Keep a steady grip on your phone near railings, and don't stop where people need to walk past.
text.geographic_location: In The Rocks, on the western side of Circular Quay, on George Street and next to First Fleet Park. Cahill Walk runs just to the south, above Circular Quay Station.
text.directions_text: Head for Circular Quay, the ferry and waterfront area at the foot of The Rocks, and head to Cahill Walk, the raised walkway above Circular Quay Station. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the museum, the wharves and the water in one frame. Switch to 2x or 3x telephoto, if your phone has it, to pick out the clock tower and the stonework. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to include more of the walkway and quay, and keep straight lines away from the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Cahill Walk (elevated walkway above Circular Quay Station, looking down toward the MCA and West Circular Quay). The museum's harbour-side building framed from above, with the ferry wharves and water in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the water's edge with a horizontal line, so the building doesn't look tilted. Put the museum in the upper-middle of the frame and let the wharves and water fill the lower part. For a second angle, go down to Circular Quay and photograph the pale Art Deco front as you would see it arriving by ferry, with the Opera House across the cove.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus. Then drag the exposure slider down a little, so the sky and water keep their colour and the building isn't washed out. Try a Live Photo to capture a ferry moving through the scene, and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. Midday light looking north can be harsh.

text.access_note: Cahill Walk is a free public walkway, but it sits above an expressway and access can change on special days such as New Year's Eve, so check on the day; the museum itself may have ticketed exhibitions, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: In Sydney the midday sun is in the northern sky, so looking north from Cahill Walk puts the light partly behind the museum; early morning or late afternoon light is gentler.
Cahill Walk is usually less busy than the quayside at street level.

name: Sydney Observatory
label: Sydney Observatory
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Observatory Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Observatory Hill Park' (way/55218510): middle (280 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/55218511: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sydney Observatory' (37 m across).
notes: Historic observatory on Observatory Hill with harbour views.

text.description:
Sydney Observatory sits on top of Observatory Hill in Millers Point, on ground that has been a windmill site, a fort and a signal station. The building you see today was designed by William Weaver and put up between 1857 and 1859. It has a time-ball tower, and the ball is still dropped every day at 1pm. It also holds the oldest telescope in regular use in Australia, a 29-centimetre refractor from 1874. The observatory was added to the New South Wales State Heritage Register in 2000.

For a phone photo, the best approach is to use the park around it rather than the building alone. The Harbour Bridge is a separate shot, taken from the rotunda on the park's western side. There, the rotunda's columns or the old fig tree make a natural frame, and Victorian terrace houses from Lower Fort Street can sit in the foreground. From the open grass you can also look across toward the bridge and the harbour, with the observatory grounds as a calmer backdrop.

The park's western aspect gives warm light on the bridge and The Rocks in the late afternoon, so plan your visit for then. Check the official site before you go if you want to go inside, as the building may not be open at all times.
text.geographic_location: Sydney Observatory is on Observatory Hill at Upper Fort Street in Millers Point, in inner Sydney. It is just above The Rocks and close to the Harbour Bridge.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops listed for this spot, so head on foot from The Rocks or Millers Point. Walk up the steps from Cumberland Street or Argyle Road into Observatory Park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the observatory from where you stand, looking west. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the bridge shot if you want the terrace houses, the bridge and the sky all in one picture. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the observatory building or the bridge on its own.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Observatory Park (by the rotunda on the western side of the park, looking back toward the observatory and the Harbour Bridge). The rotunda's columns or the old fig tree can frame the observatory and the Harbour Bridge, with Victorian terrace houses from Lower Fort Street in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines. For the observatory shot, look west from where you stand and keep the building on one of the grid lines, using the fig tree's branches at the edge of the picture if they fall naturally into view. For the bridge shot, move to the rotunda and place its columns or the fig tree's branches at the edge of the picture, with the bridge inside them. Keep the terrace rooftops low in the frame as a foreground layer. As another option, stand in the open grass of the park and shoot across it toward the bridge and the harbour, with the observatory grounds as a quieter background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the observatory or the bridge to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is washing out. Take one wide shot at 0.5x and one closer shot at 2x or more, so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or golden hour (about 4-6pm), when warm light falls on the bridge and The Rocks buildings.

text.access_note: The park around the observatory is open public space, but entry to the observatory building and any evening or tour sessions may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Observatory Park is open public parkland that can be entered without a ticket.
The observatory building may not be open to visitors at all times, and may be mainly for booked tour groups.

name: Hyde Park
label: Hyde Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Archibald Fountain' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Archibald Fountain' (relation/21781072): middle (33 m across); moved 15 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2030042: large area 'Hyde Park' (813 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Central city park with tree-lined avenues.

text.description: Hyde Park is a long, green strip of lawns and avenues on the eastern edge of Sydney's city centre. Governor Macquarie set it aside as open space in 1810, and it is the oldest public parkland in Australia. He named it after the Hyde Park in London. It covers about 16 hectares and has roughly 580 trees, and it is known for its avenues of fig trees. That is what makes it work on a phone: the trees form a leafy tunnel, and the city's buildings rise behind them. The classic view is from the Archibald Fountain at the north end of the park. Looking south, you get the Art Deco fountain in the foreground, St Mary's Cathedral behind it, and the fig-lined central path leading away into the park. The fountain sits where the two main walkways cross, so it is easy to reach and there is open space around it. Take a few steps either way to change the angle. If the main spot is busy, Sandringham Memorial Garden and Fountain is a quieter corner for portraits. Arriving early helps with crowds. Keep the fountain in the lower third of the frame, let the avenue lead the eye, and wait for walkers to give the scene some life.
text.geographic_location: Hyde Park is on the eastern edge of Sydney's city centre, between Elizabeth Street and College Street. It runs south from St James Road, and St Mary's Cathedral stands on its eastern side.
text.directions_text: From the Sydney city centre, the park is on the eastern side of the CBD, so walk to the north end of the park, near St James Road and Prince Albert Road. The Archibald Fountain is at that end, where the two main walkways cross. From the fountain, it is about 4 minutes on foot south down the central avenue to the middle of the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain with the cathedral and the avenue behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the full canopy of fig trees. Use 2x telephoto to squeeze the avenue and bring the cathedral closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (north end of the park, looking south down the central avenue). The Art Deco fountain in the foreground, with St Mary's Cathedral behind it and the fig-lined central path leading south into the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the path along the centre line, so the fig trees frame both sides. Keep the fountain low in the frame and the cathedral above it. If you want a different view, the Anzac Memorial reflected in its long Reflection Pool is a good second photo, with the city towers around the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and the water stay bright. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the water. Use portrait mode at Sandringham Memorial Garden if you are photographing people.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is described as especially lovely here. Early morning or late afternoon gives soft light, and arriving early helps with crowds.

text.access_note: Hyde Park is an open public park, but a permit may be needed for some types of organised photography in City of Sydney parks, so check the official City of Sydney site before you go if you are planning more than holiday snaps.
claims_not_in_sources: Hyde Park is an open public park that visitors can enter freely.
Water movement at the fountain can make a good Live Photo.

name: Fort Denison
label: Fort Denison
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mrs Macquarie's Chair' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mrs Macquarie's Chair' (node/13887214): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/18183678: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Denison' (102 m across).
notes: Small historic island fort in Sydney Harbour.

text.description:
Fort Denison is a small sandstone island fortress sitting in the middle of Sydney Harbour, and it makes a lovely centrepiece for a harbour photo. From here you can fit the fort, the Opera House and the Harbour Bridge into one view, which is why guides treat it as the classic postcard angle.

The island was once a rocky islet known as Pinchgut, used to punish convicts. Its stone was later quarried for Circular Quay. The fort was finished in 1857 and named after Sir William Denison, then Governor of New South Wales. Its Martello tower is the only one ever built in Australia and the last built anywhere in the British Empire. Some damage from 1942, when shells hit the tower during the midget-submarine attack on the harbour, is still visible.

For photos, the fort is a small shape on the water, so decide whether you want the whole scene or a closer shot of the tower. Early morning or around sunset, the light is warm on the Opera House and the harbour is usually calm. The island has been closed to visitors for conservation works, so you are shooting it from the shore. Check current closures before you plan your day around it.
text.geographic_location: Fort Denison is on a small island in Sydney Harbour, north-east of the Royal Botanic Garden and about a kilometre east of the Opera House.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Royal Botanic Garden in central Sydney and walk to Mrs Macquarie's Chair. The chair is on the point at the garden's harbour edge, and from there the island lies to the north-east across the water. Check the garden's own signs for the way once you are inside. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the fort, the Opera House and the Bridge together. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a closer shot of the tower. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to include the bench and the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Mrs Macquarie's Chair (carved bench on the north-east edge of the point, facing the island). Fort Denison in the middle of the harbour, with the Opera House and Harbour Bridge framed together in the same view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the fort on one of the lower grid intersections, with the Opera House and Bridge on the other side of the frame. For a quieter, lower angle across the water, try Farm Cove, which looks toward the fort with the Opera House and Bridge behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fort to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and water keep their colour. With telephoto, hold the phone steady with both hands, or rest it on something solid, to keep the shot sharp. At dusk, try night mode and stay still until it finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, when the light is warm on the Opera House and the harbour is calm.

text.access_note: Mrs Macquarie's Chair is free to visit, open daily and inside the Royal Botanic Garden, but the island itself has been closed for conservation works, so check the official site before you go.

name: Archibald Fountain
label: Archibald Fountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hyde Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hyde Park' (relation/2030042): edge nearest the subject (809 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/21781072: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Archibald Fountain' (33 m across).
notes: Bronze mythological fountain in Hyde Park.

text.description:
The Archibald Fountain stands in Hyde Park in central Sydney. It is a large bronze group in a wide granite basin, and it is easy to photograph because there is plenty of open space around it. J. F. Archibald, owner and editor of The Bulletin magazine, left money in his will for it and asked for a French artist. The sculptor François-Léon Sicard finished it in Paris in 1926, and it was unveiled in Sydney on 14 March 1932. Apollo is the central figure, with horses' heads below him spilling water into the basins. Around the large basin are groups showing Artemis, Pan and Theseus, plus six tortoises and several dolphins that all throw jets of water. That mix of bronze and moving water gives you plenty to choose from, whether you want a wide shot or a close one.

The view most photographers go for is the fountain in the foreground with the spires of St Mary's Cathedral rising behind it. For a second picture, move to a path where the fountain sits at the end of a tree-lined walk with lamps and greenery framing it. Then step in close for the bronze figures. The fountain is floodlit at night, so an evening visit gives you a different look. The water may be switched off during conservation works, so expect the occasional dry visit.
text.geographic_location: In Hyde Park, in the centre of Sydney, in an open space surrounded by formal flower gardens.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so head for Hyde Park in central Sydney. From there the fountain is to the west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main view of the fountain with the cathedral spires behind. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the bronze figures and the water jets. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only when you are close and want the whole fountain in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hyde Park (north end, on the path near the fountain, framing it against St Mary's Cathedral). The fountain in the foreground with the spires of St Mary's Cathedral rising behind it. This point gives you the fountain itself, but the cathedral backdrop is not guaranteed from here, because St Mary's Cathedral lies on the east side of the park and would be behind you. For the view with the spires rising behind the fountain, walk around to the far (west) side of the fountain and look east, then take a few steps until the spires sit neatly behind the sculpture. Check the map to confirm your position.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the verticals straight, with the fountain in the lower part of the frame and the spires above it. Take a wide shot first, then move in for close-ups of the bronze figures and plinths. For a different picture, shoot down a tree-lined path with the fountain at the end and the pedestrian lamps and greenery framing it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sculpture or water to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the spray does not turn white. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the water. After dark, hold the phone steady against a railing or your body and use night mode.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Just before sunset, when the light sparkles on the water spray. After dark the fountain is floodlit, which makes a good night-mode picture.

text.access_note: The fountain is in an open public park; check the official site before you go in case works or a switched-off fountain affect your visit.
